title: The end of the age of heroes
gist: Noah Smith argues that OpenAI's Astra solving ten open math and theoretical CS problems ends mathematics' 'age of heroes', because AI is not a replacement worker but a replacement world-mind that removes the single-human-brain bottleneck on ideas. He predicts mathematicians keep their jobs — their entire U.S. salary bill is a $4-5 billion GDP rounding error — but shift from discoverers to professional understanders of machine-generated results.

insights.claim: OpenAI's model Astra solved ten major outstanding problems in math and theoretical computer science, an event treated by consensus as a set of stunning breakthroughs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete capability datapoint for anyone underwriting AI-model differentiation: frontier reasoning is now producing verifiable research output, not just benchmarks.
insights.quote: OpenAI announced that its new model, Astra, managed to solve ten major outstanding problems in math and theoretical computer science.
insights.locator: This week marked another important such moment

insights.claim: The most prominent skeptic of AI in frontier math research, Toronto's Daniel Litt, publicly conceded his bet against AI producing Annals-quality number theory papers, saying remaining gaps are only a matter of time.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Skeptic capitulation is a leading indicator; expert consensus on AI research capability is repricing faster than most AI-exposure models assume.
insights.quote: The models don’t yet seem able to do certain kinds of high quality research, but I also expect this is a matter of (not too much) time.
insights.locator: The University of Toronto’s Daniel Litt

insights.claim: The concrete terms on the table were AI producing Annals-quality number theory papers within five years at an inference budget at or below $100k per paper.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Gives a price anchor for 'research-grade' inference: sub-$100k/paper implies enormous compute demand per unit of scientific output.
insights.quote: I bet @littmath that in 5 years AI will be able to produce Annals-quality Number Theory papers at an inference budget at or below $100k/paper, at 3:1 odds in my favor.
insights.locator: Tamay Besiroglu @tamaybes

insights.claim: A live limitation thesis remains that LLMs excel at combining the entire existing literature but still fall short of truly novel leaps of insight.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The bear case on AI research value is now narrow and specific — novelty, not recall — and is the thing to test when evaluating AI-for-science claims.
insights.locator: Some people have argued that AI is good

insights.claim: Working mathematicians are describing the AI math breakthroughs in the language of spiritual crisis rather than tooling, indicating disruption is hitting identity and not just workflow.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Emotional capitulation inside an elite profession is an early template for how other high-status knowledge fields will react to AI displacement.
insights.quote: I am suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments. I have been screaming internally for days.
insights.locator: The Dark Night of Mathematics

insights.claim: A confrontational counter-strategy is emerging in which mathematicians are urged to refuse collaboration with AI companies and preserve current research practice, a boycott the author judges extremely unlikely to work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Expect labor-side resistance to AI in academia to be loud but ineffective; do not price in successful professional gatekeeping.
insights.locator: Math PhD student Tasmin Chu

insights.claim: The institutional machinery of mathematics — training grad students, choosing problems, collaboration, theory-building — will have to be overhauled even for mathematicians who reject the despair narrative.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Watch university math departments and funding structures as the first observable site of AI-driven restructuring in higher education.
insights.locator: Even the mathematicians who don’t share Hampshire’s despair

insights.claim: A freshly minted Fields Medalist took a job at OpenAI, illustrating that top mathematical talent is migrating to AI labs rather than resisting them.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Talent flow is a cheap proxy for where value is accruing; elite academic capture by labs strengthens their moat.
insights.locator: Jacob Tsimerman, who just won the Fields Medal

insights.claim: The loss that matters to mathematicians is the loss of problem-solving as an activity, not the loss of truth: if the struggle disappears, many practitioners may simply stop wanting to do the work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Motivation collapse, not unemployment, may be the binding constraint on retaining human experts in AI-augmented fields.
insights.quote: There are many people whose primary enjoyment of math comes through problem solving in one of its incarnations. If that disappears, that is not a trivial issue and many of them might not want to do it anymore.
insights.locator: I do not do mathematics only to find truth

insights.claim: Human beings have always functioned as edge compute — gathering slightly novel local data and reporting it back to a central world-mind that was society itself, made of corporations, governments, universities and human networks.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for valuing AI: the bottleneck being removed is societal coordination bandwidth, not individual labor hours.
insights.quote: In essence, humans were always what we now call edge compute — little devices that reported data back to a central world-mind.

insights.claim: AI should be understood as a replacement for the societal world-mind rather than as a replacement for an individual worker, because it integrates the findings of many humans and sensors into one general picture of the world.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI TAM from wage replacement to coordination-layer replacement, which implies far larger and more concentrated economic rents.
insights.quote: AI is really a new world-mind — a technology that takes the accumulated findings of individual humans (or robots, or other sensors) and integrates them into a general picture of the world.
insights.locator: We normally think of AI as something that replaces

insights.claim: Heroic individual genius was an artifact of an information bottleneck: every idea entering the collective had to be comprehensible to, and therefore first conceivable by, a single human brain — a constraint AI removes.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If the single-brain comprehension constraint really is the binding one, AI-native research pipelines can produce results no human org could have generated at any budget.
insights.locator: But that heroism was necessary because

insights.claim: The migration from human institutions to AI as coordinating superintelligence is analogous to derivatives moving from over-the-counter bilateral trading to central clearinghouses after Dodd-Frank.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The clearinghouse analogy predicts centralization, standardization and a small number of systemically important AI intermediaries — with the attendant concentration risk.
insights.quote: The shift from human organizations to AI as our coordinating superintelligence feels a little like the shift from OTC information exchange to a central clearinghouse.
insights.locator: I actually think of a financial analogy here

insights.claim: Every scientist and businessperson is now effectively writing training data for AI whether or not they intend to, because published findings and expressed perspectives feed the models.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports the view that proprietary, non-public data streams are the durable asset; anything published is already an input to somebody else's model.
insights.quote: every scientist and every businessperson is just writing for the AIs now, whether they intend to or not.

insights.claim: Fields where mathematics is an input rather than an output — economics in particular — get an immediate productivity windfall as the theory-writing constraint is removed and effort shifts to data and empirics.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Look for measurable acceleration in empirical output from math-constrained disciplines; it is the first place AI-for-science ROI should show up.

insights.claim: Claims for the size of the AI science acceleration range from a 100x boost to something as modest as 1.5x, and which one obtains is still genuinely unresolved.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The spread between 1.5x and 100x is the entire investment case for AI-for-science; treat confident point estimates in either direction as unsupported.
insights.quote: AI will lead us to the new age of mathematical discoveries and boost science progress 100x.
insights.locator: Przemek Chojecki writes

insights.claim: AI lowers the cost of solving any given math problem but simultaneously enables the creation of far harder problems, so difficulty migrates upward rather than disappearing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Argues against a saturation thesis: demand for compute-intensive research does not fall as capability rises, it moves to a harder frontier.
insights.quote: But AI will also come up with — and will allow humans to come up with — much harder problems than have been created so far.
insights.locator: AI will make any given math problem a lot easier

themes.theme: Economics of employing humans after obsolescence

insights.claim: Total academic mathematician salaries in the U.S. are at most roughly $4-5 billion, comparable to national spending on bowling alleys or Halloween candy, so society can afford to keep employing them purely for human understanding.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A general template: professions whose entire wage bill is a GDP rounding error will survive automation on cultural grounds, not economic ones — useful when handicapping displacement narratives.
insights.quote: The sum total of all of the salaries of academic mathematicians in the U.S. is maybe $4-5 billion dollars at most. That’s a rounding error on our GDP — it’s about what we spend on bowling alleys, or Halloween candy.
insights.locator: The reason is that mathematicians, as a class

insights.claim: Most frontier mathematical research arguably does not produce value for money in economic terms outside of some cryptography and occasional physics applications, meaning it was already being subsidized as an intrinsic good.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that AI automating research immediately translates into measurable GDP gains in that field.

insights.claim: The binding constraint after AI solves problems becomes human comprehension of the solutions, which preserves a prestigious role for experts as professional understanders rather than discoverers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Verification, interpretation and comprehension layers are where residual human economic value concentrates in an AI-saturated knowledge industry.

insights.claim: Unassisted human problem-solving will persist as sport and hobby, in the same way sprinters and woodworkers persist despite cars and machine tools.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Predicts durable niche demand for 'human-made' intellectual work, an analogue of artisanal premium markets in goods.
insights.quote: Just as there are still sprinters even though humans can’t outrun cars, there will still be mathletes.
